F.1-1.label: Function Meaning
F.1-1.example: Each student → one birth month, so it is a function.

F.1-2.label: Spotting Functions
F.1-2.example: (2, 5), (2, 7), (3, 1): not a function; input 2 has two outputs.

F.1-3.label: Vertical Line Test
F.1-3.example: A circle is not a function: one vertical line can hit it twice.

F.1-6.label: Function Notation
F.1-6.example: f(x) = −2x + 5: f(6) = −7, so the point is (6, −7).

F.1-7.label: Behavior at Points
F.1-7.example: Tank: 100 gal at 8 min, 75 gal at 10 min → drains 12.5 gal/min.

F.1-8.label: Tricky Functions
F.1-8.example: x = y² is not a function: input 4 gives y = 2 and y = −2.

F.3-1.label: Linear or Nonlinear
F.3-1.example: y = x² + 1 is nonlinear (it curves); y = 3x − 2 is linear.

F.3-2.label: Types of Slope
F.3-2.example: Rises: positive. Falls: negative. Flat: zero. Vertical: undefined.

F.3-3.label: Slope-Intercept Form
F.3-3.example: y = −x + 8: m = −1 is the slope, b = 8 is the y-intercept.

F.3-4.label: Finding m and b
F.3-4.example: Up 8, right 2 → slope = 4; crosses the y-axis at −3, so b = −3.

F.3-5.label: Changing m and b
F.3-5.example: y = 2x + 1 → y = 5x − 3: steeper, and crosses 4 units lower.

F.3-7.label: Real-World Meaning
F.3-7.example: Gym y = 25x + 50: $25 per month, plus a $50 sign-up fee.

F.3-8.label: Constant Rate Proof
F.3-8.example: y = 4x + 3: each time x goes up 1, y always goes up exactly 4.

F.2-1.label: Rate & Start Value
F.2-1.example: x: 0, 1, 2 and y: 7, 9, 11 → rate of change 2, initial value 7

F.2-2.label: Meaning in Context
F.2-2.example: Taxi y = 2.50x + 4: $2.50 per mile; $4 is the starting fee.

F.2-3.label: Basic Comparison
F.2-3.example: y = 3x + 1 grows faster; y = 2x + 7 starts higher.

F.2-4.label: Comparing Formats
F.2-4.example: Graph slope 4, table slope 3, y = −2x + 10 → order: 4, 3, −2

F.2-5.label: Trends & Predictions
F.2-5.example: Battery y = −0.6x + 100: negative trend; 40% left after 100 minutes.

F.2-7.label: Evidence-Based Predictions
F.2-7.example: 200 m race: Jon (d = 7t) finishes at 28.6 s, Mia (d = 5t + 30) at 34 s → Jon wins.

F.2-8.label: Points in Context
F.2-8.example: Gift card y = −15x + 240: (20, −60) makes no sense; balance can't be negative.

F.4-1.label: Is It Linear?
F.4-1.example: Taxi: $3 plus $2 per mile is linear; it goes up the same $2 each mile.

F.4-2.label: Rate & Initial Value
F.4-2.example: $45, $57, $69 at weeks 0, 1, 2 → $12 per week, initial value $45

F.4-3.label: Rise Over Run
F.4-3.example: Falls 8 over a run of 4: slope −8/4 = −2. Horizontal: 0. Vertical: undefined.

F.4-4.label: Writing Equations
F.4-4.example: Starts at 80 ft, drops 4 ft each second → y = −4x + 80

F.4-7.label: Multi-Step Models
F.4-7.example: 2 h: $170, 5 h: $335 → y = 55x + 60; a $500 job takes 8 hours.

F.4-9.label: Linear vs. Other Functions
F.4-9.example: +$10 each week is linear (constant rate); doubling each week is not.

F.5-1.label: Up, Down, or Flat
F.5-1.example: Graph falls from 25 to 40 seconds → the height is decreasing then.

F.5-2.label: Straight or Curved
F.5-2.example: A straight piece of a graph is linear; a curved piece is non-linear.

F.5-3.label: Story to Graph
F.5-3.example: Fill tub, take bath, drain → graph goes up, stays flat, then down to 0.

F.5-4.label: Simple Sketches
F.5-4.example: Kite rises steadily 2 min, then holds 3 min → slant up, then flat.

F.5-5.label: Interval Language
F.5-5.example: Increasing 0 to 2 h, constant 2 to 3 h, decreasing 3 to 5 h

F.5-6.label: Rate of Change Check
F.5-6.example: Up 10, then 20, then 30 m each minute → rate changes, so non-linear.

F.5-7.label: Multi-Part Sketches
F.5-7.example: Train speeds up, cruises, then slows to a stop → speed graph: up, flat, down to 0.

F.5-8.label: Graph Stories
F.5-8.example: Gas graph: down = driving, flat = parked, jump up = filled the tank.

F.5-9.label: Curved Graphs
F.5-9.example: Ball drops 5, 15, then 25 m each second: rate grows, so the graph curves.

SP.1-1.label: Making Scatter Plots
SP.1-1.example: Week 1: 26 wpm, week 6: 36 wpm → plot points (1, 26) and (6, 36).

SP.1-2.label: Direction of Association
SP.1-2.example: Hotter days, less hot cocoa sold → negative association.

SP.1-3.label: Linear or Non-Linear
SP.1-3.example: Bacteria double every hour → the points curve, so non-linear.

SP.1-4.label: Clusters & Outliers
SP.1-4.example: Clusters at 4–6 h and 18–21 h; (20, 90) is an outlier.

SP.1-5.label: Strong or Weak
SP.1-5.example: Points stay very close to an upward line → strong positive association.

SP.1-6.label: Explaining Outliers
SP.1-6.example: (3, 35) is an outlier: the pattern predicts about 11 min for 3 miles, not 35.

SP.1-7.label: Comparing Plots
SP.1-7.example: Lemonade: strong positive. Soup: weak negative (trends down but zigzags).

SP.1-8.label: Full Analysis
SP.1-8.example: Screen time vs. sleep: negative, two clusters, one outlier; a link, not proof of cause.

SP.1-9.label: Real-World Reasoning
SP.1-9.example: Height from age 0 to 30 is non-linear: growth slows, then stops.

SP.3-1.label: Slope Meaning
SP.3-1.example: y = −8x + 100: the battery drops 8 percentage points each hour.

SP.3-2.label: Y-Intercept Meaning
SP.3-2.example: y = 15x + 40: Malik started with $40 when x = 0 weeks.

SP.3-5.label: Detailed Predictions
SP.3-5.example: Candle y = −1.5x + 24: starts 24 cm tall, burns out (y = 0) at 16 hours.

SP.3-6.label: Solving for Unknowns
SP.3-6.example: y = mx + 15 through (4, 75) → m = 15; y = 165 at x = 10 hours

SP.3-8.label: Extrapolation
SP.3-8.example: y = 2.5x + 29: age 30 → 104 in., not reasonable since growth stops in the teens.

SP.4-2.label: Joint & Marginal
SP.4-2.example: Joint: 25 seventh graders skip breakfast. Marginal: 60 seventh graders in all.

SP.4-4.label: Row & Column Percents
SP.4-4.example: 12 of the 80 who live over 2 miles away bike: 12 ÷ 80 = 15%

SP.4-5.label: Spotting Associations
SP.4-5.example: Curfew: 42 ÷ 60 = 70% get 8+ h; no curfew: 30 ÷ 75 = 40% → association

SP.4-6.label: Meaning in Context
SP.4-6.example: 12 ÷ 80 = 0.15 means 15% of shoppers under 25 paid cash.

SP.4-7.label: Justifying Associations
SP.4-7.example: 48% of 2+ hour gamers vs. 70% of others turn work in on time → association.

SP.4-8.label: Strength of Association
SP.4-8.example: 40 ÷ 64 and 45 ÷ 72 both = 62.5% like dogs → no association with handedness.

SP.2-1.label: Drawing the Line
SP.2-1.example: Draw the line through the middle: about half the points above, half below.

SP.2-2.label: Trend, Not Every Point
SP.2-2.example: A line of best fit can miss most points; it shows the overall trend.

SP.2-3.label: Judging the Fit
SP.2-3.example: Every point within 0.5 of the line → good fit; all points above it → poor fit.

SP.2-6.label: Outlier Effects
SP.2-6.example: One very high last point pulls the line's right end up, so it is too flat.

SP.2-7.label: Comparing Lines
SP.2-7.example: Line A: all points within 1 book. Line B: up to 5 off → A is better.

SP.2-8.label: Model Strength & Limits
SP.2-8.example: Close points → strong model. Limit: y = 5x + 60 predicts 105 at 9 h, above 100.
